summary:
Omsk Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, and the sources reviewed for this division record no oblast-specific legal or enforcement divergence from it. Visitors to Omsk therefore face the same regime as elsewhere in Russia.

Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised under Russian law. Same-sex marriage and legal gender transition are banned: gender-affirming healthcare was effectively prohibited in 2023, and in the same year the Supreme Court designated the 'international LGBT movement' an extremist organisation, a designation that applies in Omsk Oblast as it does across the federation.

The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia, version 2.0 of June 2025, applies this framework in assessing protection claims and records that between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement. The note provides no Omsk-level detail.

Enforcement is active and escalating. Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions for participation in the designated movement or for displaying its symbols since the November 2023 ruling, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison. In the same period HRW documented 81 people found guilty across 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 of the code of administrative offences for displaying banned LGBT symbols, most often on social media.

Public expression carries direct penalties. 'Gay propaganda' offences can attract fines of up to 400,000 rubles (approximately £3,600) or 15 days' detention for individuals, and the expanded propaganda statutes reach speech that is said to 'justify' gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, detention and deportation.
tangentialFactors:
The Supreme Court's designation of the 'international LGBT movement' as extremist has been enforced within days of the ruling: The Guardian reported on 17 January 2024 that masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow venues within 48 hours, with about 100 patrons at one bar ordered to face walls, searched and photographed.

Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years preceding.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented in the region. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 on a transgender woman held for nine months in a conversion-therapy facility near Novosibirsk, where she was forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping.

The Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to people fleeing Russia on the basis of these laws. The US State Department's travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries explicit warnings directed at LGBT travellers.
localsOnly:
Residents of Omsk Oblast face the same legal exposure as elsewhere in Russia: participation in the designated movement or display of its symbols can be prosecuted as extremism, while administrative liability under article 20.3 has been applied to 81 people across 98 cases since January 2024, most of them for online posts.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable, and the 2023 bans on gender-affirming care and on 'gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents' leave no lawful domestic route to transition or to updated identity documents.

Same-sex marriage is not recognised. The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, with a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as 'a second-class citizen' after the designation.

The UK Home Office note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the standard for UK asylum claims. The Russian-language service of the UK asylum framework applies this assessment; there is no parallel route of protection within Russia itself.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records any Omsk Oblast-specific court decision, raid, prosecution or local regulation concerning LGBT people or gender identity. The UK Home Office country policy note explicitly records no oblast-level detail, and the Human Rights Watch enforcement figures are national. Whether local police practice in Omsk differs from the national pattern is unresolved.

The inventory does not state whether the 101 extremism convictions or the 81 administrative guilty findings under article 20.3 include any individuals in Omsk Oblast; the figures are national aggregates and their regional distribution is not sourced.

Whether Omsk's medical institutions had begun closing gender-affirming services in practice before the 2023 national ban, and what private or informal care remains available in the oblast, is not addressed by the sources reviewed.

The status of asylum or protection applications by Russian nationals and third-country nationals located in Omsk Oblast is not covered in the inventory.
